title: The Economist - nearly right but crucially wrong about learning, gives 'learning-focused schools' something to think about, too.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton reviews The Economist education special of July 2024 and finds it frustrating for four reasons: it contradicts itself, treats evidence selectively, conflates skills with woolliness, and surrounds its back-to-basics message with a long list of systemic problems it never connects to the message. He argues that numeracy and literacy cannot be learned without the skills they contain, so setting skills against basics is a false opposition. Drawing on his earlier posts about brain energy, he compares back to basics to a political slogan that ignores complexity and so saves mental effort. He then turns the critique on his own camp, warning that calling a school learning-focused can become an equally empty bumper sticker. His conclusion is that the label should be an invitation to dig into what learning is and what affects it.
points: The Economist special praises evidence yet leans on hedges such as in theory or not yet clear when ideas it favours lack support.
Literacy and numeracy depend on skills as much as on factual knowledge, so dismissing skills as faddish misunderstands the basics themselves.
Skelton likens back to basics to a sticky slogan that saves brain energy by ignoring the complexity of malnutrition, poverty, teacher recruitment and the rest.
He accepts that rigour and strong numeracy and literacy matter, but argues that a narrow basics-only definition of the student we are developing is not enough today.
A learning-focused school that is only a poster or tagline commits the same sin of simplicity, so the label must prompt real exploration of the factors that help or hinder learning.
quotes: Skills are not, by definition, ‘woolly’ or ‘faddish’. Even the two kinds of ‘back to basics’ learning the writers want us to get back to - numeracy and literacy - simply cannot be learned without crucial numeracy and literacy skills being learned alongside the equally important knowledge they both contain.
In other words, ideas without evidence are ok if they want them to be but ‘faddish’ if they don’t.
It sounds good, ignores complexity, and saves brain energy. We need to do better than this.
The Economist is nearly right but, in the end, worryingly wrong. I am in favour of rigour, too. I am against woolly thinking where it should not be woolly.

What made The Economist’s special so unrewarding for me is that it set out two ideas - ‘Back to Basics’ and then some of the many systemic factors that affect schooling - without really linking them together and letting them influence each other.
Declaring ourselves to be a learning-focused school or organisation isn’t enough if it ends up being no more than a bumper sticker or a slogan in a hallway or on a cap.
